Chenxi Feng

Ph.D. Student · Atmospheric Sciences · Cornell University

Hello! I am a climate scientist, focusing on future climate mitigation solutions like solar geoengineering and carbon dioxide removal. My research integrates Earth system modeling, observation-model fusion, and machine learning to assess the efficacy and risks of climate intervention pathways.

I'm currently a Ph.D. student at Cornell University majored in Atmospheric Sciences, working with Dr. Daniele Visioni. I graduated from Nanjing University in 2024 with a B.S. in Atmospheric Sciences.

Multi-band Fusion for Spaceborne Methane Detection

Core Knowledge Gap

Operational methane detection stuck in bottleneck: existing methods fail to maintain high-accuracy emission quantification under real-world observation noise without incurring prohibitive compute costs.

Key Achievements

  • Developed an effective multi-band fusion algorithm (Fused-MF) to maximize methane emission signals.
  • Proposed algorithm demonstrated superior methane emission rate quantification accuracy compared with traditional single-band methods.

Aerosol-Induced Bias Calibration for Methane Detection

Core Knowledge Gap

Lack of an efficient and fast calibration algorithm to eliminate aerosol-induced bias in methane emission retrieval from hyperspectral instruments.

Key Achievements

  • Developed an efficient aerosol-calibrated methane retrieval algorithm (ACMF).
  • Proposed algorithm demonstrates superior retrieval accuracy and robustness under the interruption of aerosol radiative forcing.

Intrinsic Temperature Response of Microbial Respiratory Soil Organic Carbon Loss

Core Knowledge Gap

Mechanistic understanding remains critically lacking regarding why soil organic carbon loss via microbial respiration exhibits divergent responses to warming, ranging from acceleration to attenuation.

Key Findings

  • Global convergence exist toward kinetically acceleration in microbial respiratory soil organic carbon loss under warming.
  • Observed divergent temperature responses are largely confounded by substrate availability.
  • Current observations and models significantly underestimate potential microbial respiratory soil organic carbon loss under warming.

Related Publications
